payload.executive_summary: Candidate B2B adopts the plugin-based build architecture (O2) with a hybrid milestone strategy. Phase A front-loads the design and implementation of the core build engine, shared build context, and plugin lifecycle (ingest → transform → render → emit), establishing the foundational plugin API contract. Phase B delivers feature plugins incrementally: first ingestion + Markdown rendering (R1–R6), then link/backlink resolution (R9, R10), tag extraction and pages (R11–R13), search index (R7, R8), and theme/navigation (R17). Phase C adds SHOULD/COULD plugins for wiki-links (R15), base-URL rewriting (R19), and incremental builds (R23). High HITL strictness is applied throughout because the plugin API is a critical decision point—an incorrect contract causes cascading rework across all feature plugins. Security governance is elevated: each plugin's template output is reviewed for XSS (K7), user-provided plugins are sandboxed (K19), and all plugin dependencies are pinned (K21). This candidate is best suited for projects expected to grow beyond initial scope, supporting multiple Markdown flavors, additional output formats, and community contributions.

architecture_choice.rationale: O2's plugin-based architecture provides the extensibility needed for long-term growth (multiple Markdown flavors, community plugins, additional output formats) while keeping each feature isolated and independently testable. The upfront cost of designing a stable plugin API and shared build context is justified by the branch's expectation that the project will evolve beyond its initial scope. Compared to O1 (monolithic), O2 enables swapping individual features without rewriting the core. Compared to O3 (SSG-based), O2 avoids tight coupling to an external SSG's release cadence. Compared to O4 (multi-stage pipeline), O2 achieves similar separation of concerns without the complexity of intermediate file-based artifacts and cache invalidation. The hybrid milestone strategy mitigates O2's main risk—plugin API instability—by designing the API holistically in Phase A before iterating features as isolated plugins in Phase B.
architecture_choice.high_level_dataflow: CLI invocation → Core Build Engine (C9) loads config and discovers/registers plugins → Ingest hook: Ingestion Plugin (C11) scans source directory and populates Shared Build Context (C10) with note records → Transform hook: Metadata & Tag Plugin (C12) extracts/normalizes tags; Link Resolution & Backlink Plugin (C13) detects links and computes backlinks; both write to C10 → Render hook: Markdown Render Plugin (C14) converts Markdown to HTML in C10; Theme/Template Plugin (C15) produces final page outputs; Search Index Plugin (C16) builds client-side search index → Emit hook: Emit Plugin (C17) writes pages, assets, and search index to output directory → Static site served to browser with client-side search runtime.

Integration smoke tests validating plugin loading, lifecycle hook execution order, and shared context read/write round-trip.
Plugin API documentation and contract specification (versioned).

Shared context API supports CRUD for note records, tags, and link edges; verified by unit tests.
CLI accepts input/output paths and config, invokes engine, and exits 0 with no-op plugins.
Plugin ordering respects declared dependencies; verified by integration test with ordering assertions.

decision_log.question: Which architecture option should be selected for this candidate?
decision_log.choice: O2 — Plugin-based build core with lifecycle hooks and shared build context.
decision_log.rationale: O2 provides the best extensibility for a project expected to grow beyond initial scope. The plugin model isolates features, enabling independent development, testing, and community contributions. The hybrid milestone strategy mitigates the upfront API design risk by front-loading it in Phase A with HITL review.
alternatives_considered: O1 — Monolithic CLI pipeline: simpler but harder to extend safely.
O3 — Existing SSG (Eleventy): faster time-to-value but couples to SSG release cadence and limits custom backlink/wiki-link logic.
O4 — Multi-stage pipeline with intermediate artifacts: good for incremental builds but adds cache management complexity without the plugin extensibility benefits.
what_would_change_this_decision: Project scope is confirmed to be small and fixed (no future growth) — O1 would be simpler.
Team already uses Eleventy and wants minimal custom code — O3 would be faster.
Incremental build performance is the top priority over extensibility — O4 would be more natural.

evidence_pointers.note: Plugin-based architecture definition with lifecycle hooks.
Branch B2 selects O2 with hybrid milestone strategy.

decision_log.question: What milestone strategy should be used?
decision_log.choice: Hybrid: big-bang foundation (Phase A) followed by thin-slice feature plugins (Phase B) and extended plugins (Phase C).
decision_log.rationale: The plugin API must be designed holistically before features can be delivered as isolated plugins. Phase A establishes the contract; Phase B delivers MUST requirements incrementally; Phase C adds SHOULD/COULD features. This balances upfront design rigor with iterative delivery.
alternatives_considered: Pure thin-slice: risk of API redesign when later plugins reveal contract gaps.
Pure big-bang: delays all user-visible functionality until the entire system is built.
what_would_change_this_decision: Plugin API is already proven from a prior project — skip Phase A and go pure thin-slice.
Stakeholder demands earliest possible demo — compress Phase A and overlap with Phase B1.

evidence_pointers.note: Hybrid strategy specified in branch definition.

decision_log.question: What governance posture should be applied?
decision_log.choice: Sandboxed tooling with high HITL strictness.
decision_log.rationale: The plugin API design in Phase A is a critical decision point — incorrect API design causes cascading rework across all feature plugins. High HITL strictness ensures human review at key architectural junctures. Sandboxed tooling limits blast radius of plugin execution.
alternatives_considered: Standard HITL strictness: acceptable for O1 but insufficient for the API design risk in O2.
Unrestricted tooling: unacceptable given plugin extensibility increases attack surface (K19, K21).
what_would_change_this_decision: Plugin API is locked and proven stable — reduce HITL strictness to standard.
All plugins are first-party only with no user-provided plugins — relax sandboxing.

evidence_pointers.note: High HITL strictness and sandboxed tooling specified.
Template injection risk elevated due to plugin extensibility.

decision_log.question: How should XSS risk (K7) be mitigated in a plugin architecture?
decision_log.choice: Enforce HTML sanitization in the shared build context API; each plugin's template output is reviewed for XSS before merge.
decision_log.rationale: In O2, multiple plugins contribute HTML content to the shared context. Centralizing sanitization in the context API ensures consistent protection regardless of which plugin produces the content. Per-plugin review catches edge cases the central sanitizer might miss.
alternatives_considered: Per-plugin sanitization only: inconsistent and error-prone.
Disallow raw HTML entirely: too restrictive for advanced users.
what_would_change_this_decision: Trust model changes to 'all content is trusted' (personal-only use) — relax sanitization.
A proven sanitization library is integrated at the template engine level — simplify to engine-level only.

evidence_pointers.note: XSS/content injection risk with sanitization mitigation.

decision_log.question: How should plugin dependency and supply-chain risk (K21) be managed?
decision_log.choice: Pin all plugin dependencies; run vulnerability scanning in CI; prefer well-maintained libraries.
decision_log.rationale: O2's plugin model increases the number of dependencies compared to O1. Pinning and scanning are essential to prevent supply-chain attacks. The elevated risk posture for this branch explicitly calls for dependency pinning.
alternatives_considered: Use only built-in/first-party plugins with no external dependencies: limits extensibility.
Allow floating dependency versions: faster updates but higher supply-chain risk.
what_would_change_this_decision: Project moves to a vendored/zero-dependency model — scanning becomes less critical.
A trusted plugin registry with automated security review is established.

evidence_pointers.note: Dependency supply-chain risk with pinning and scanning mitigation.

decision_log.question: How should user-provided plugins and templates be handled for security (K19)?
decision_log.choice: Sandbox user-provided plugins; limit template customization to safe configuration (CSS variables, allowed template slots); lint templates.
decision_log.rationale: Plugin extensibility is O2's key advantage but also its key security risk. Sandboxing prevents arbitrary code execution from untrusted plugins. Template linting catches injection patterns before they reach production output.
alternatives_considered: No user-provided plugins: eliminates risk but defeats O2's purpose.
Full unrestricted plugin execution: unacceptable security posture.
what_would_change_this_decision: All plugins are authored by the core team only — relax sandboxing to code review only.
A formal plugin certification process is established with automated security analysis.

evidence_pointers.note: Template/theme injection risk elevated due to plugin extensibility.

decision_log.question: How should privacy risk (K8) be addressed given no access control?
decision_log.choice: Accept risk with documentation disclaimer and a build-time 'publish warning' feature that alerts users when building for public deployment.
decision_log.rationale: Access control is a non-goal. The most practical mitigation is user awareness: a build-time warning when the output is configured for public hosting reminds users to review content for sensitive information.
alternatives_considered: Ignore the risk entirely: unacceptable for a tool that publishes personal notes.
what_would_change_this_decision: Stakeholder requires content redaction features — add a redaction plugin.
Target audience shifts to enterprise teams — access control becomes necessary.

evidence_pointers.note: Critical privacy leakage risk due to static output without access control.

supplemental_evaluations.title: Plugin API Stability Risk Assessment
supplemental_evaluations.notes: The plugin API (C9/C10 interfaces IF9–IF15) is the single most critical design artifact in this candidate. If the API contract changes after Phase B plugins are built, rework cascades across all plugins. Mitigation: Phase A includes HITL review of the API contract, versioned documentation, and integration smoke tests. The exit criteria for M1 require Tech Lead approval of the plugin API before proceeding to Phase B. Residual risk: unforeseen requirements in Phase C (e.g., incremental build hooks) may require API extensions. Recommendation: design the API with explicit extension points and a versioning scheme from the start.

evidence.note: Plugin API evolution and breaking changes listed as a risk of O2.
evidence.quote: Plugin API and data model may evolve, causing breaking changes and ecosystem churn

evidence.note: Branch risk posture acknowledges API design as critical decision point.

supplemental_evaluations.title: Security Posture Under Plugin Architecture
supplemental_evaluations.notes: O2 elevates three security risks compared to O1: (1) K7 XSS — multiple plugins produce HTML, requiring centralized sanitization in C10. (2) K19 template injection — plugin extensibility means user-provided templates could inject scripts; sandboxing and linting are required. (3) K21 supply chain — more dependencies from plugins; all must be pinned and scanned. The branch risk posture explicitly addresses all three. HITL triggers include any decision affecting security boundaries (raw HTML, template execution, third-party libraries).

supplemental_evaluations.title: Acceptance Test Coverage for SHOULD Requirements
supplemental_evaluations.notes: Alignment warning AL001 (referenced in branch acceptance strategy) notes that SHOULD requirements (R15–R22) lack dedicated acceptance tests in the canonical AT set. This candidate addresses the gap by: (1) adding plugin-isolation tests in M7 to cover R15 and R19 indirectly, (2) including R22 performance validation in M5, and (3) covering R17 navigation and R21 GFM in M6 exit criteria. Formal acceptance tests for remaining SHOULD requirements should be created as corresponding plugins are delivered. This is tracked as W1.
